## From a new dataset to documentation, fast

The goal is to get from a raw file to *stable, publishable documentation* with as
little hand work as possible. datagoodr does this by combining two things: the
**formex** typing engine, which classifies every column automatically, and a set
of **default guide templates**, which know how to render each type. Put them
together and a brand-new dataset has a first, complete Research Guide before you
have written a single label.

```{r render}
dgf <- create_dgf(raw_data, file = "DGF", open = FALSE)  # type + profile
create_rg(dgf, file = "research-guide")                  # scaffold the guide
```

`create_rg()` builds a self-contained report pointed at your DGF. Because the DGF
already carries every column's profile (the `rg_*` cells), the guide renders from
the governance file alone — the raw data is not needed again.

## One guide, a different style for each type

A good data profile does not look the same for every column. A distribution of
incomes wants a histogram; a set of regions wants to show relative share; a date
column wants to show coverage over time. The renderer dispatches on each column's
type and chooses the matching style:

| type | reporting style | what it shows |
|---|---|---|
| **number** | histogram + quantile table | shape, center, spread, tails |
| **categorical** | treemap + frequency table | levels sized by share |
| **temporal (calendar)** | calendar heat-map | coverage and density over dates |
| **temporal (grain)** | period bars | counts by year / quarter / month |
| **boolean** | two-bar chart | the TRUE / FALSE split |
| **text** | word cloud + length summary | vocabulary and typical length |

So the *same* guide, built from the *same* DGF, presents an income column, a
region column, and a founding-date column each in the form that reads best —
without you choosing any of it.

## Typing quality drives guide quality

Because the style follows the type, the guide is only as good as the typing. A
column mistyped as text renders as a word cloud when it wanted a histogram. This
is why datagoodr records *how confident* each guess is and leaves the final say
to you: confirm the easy ones, correct the few that matter, and the guide
re-renders in the right style.

For how the types are guessed — the two-axis leaf, the honesty columns, and the
storage-safety gate — see **Guessing Data Types**.

## Iterate

The guide is regenerated from the DGF, so improving documentation is a loop: curate
a label or fix a type, re-profile with `update_dgf()`, and re-render. Nothing you
hand-edited is lost. For customizing layout, formatting, and narrative around the
generated sections, `create_rg()` scaffolds an editable project (a Quarto
document plus a `DG.R` you can override) — see the package reference.
